transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I didn't actually want to take time out of my schedule to be here, to be completely honest with you, because as a chief executive, my days are scheduled down to the absolute minute. I have back-to-back meetings, but I suppose I had to come in because... well, it’s the conference room. The main one on the executive floor, the one right next to my office. I just... I keep hearing people talking about me. 

And it’s not just normal office gossip, it’s coming right through the walls. Or from my phone. My phone will be completely powered down, I mean completely off, sitting face down on my desk, not a single light on, and I can still hear them coming through the speaker. It's the board members, mostly, and some of my senior staff. They just keep saying these awful things, saying that I’m ruining the company, that I'm destroying everything we've built, dissecting and criticizing every single strategic decision I've made this year. 

And the thing is, Doctor, it sounds so incredibly clear. It's not muffled by the drywall or anything. It's so loud and clear that I actually answer them back. I'll be sitting there defending my quarterly projections out loud, telling them exactly why my financial strategy is sound, and I'll be halfway through my sentence, really getting into my defense, before I look around and realize... no one else heard it. The room is completely empty. But they're right there, I hear them, and it's just so impossible to get any work done when my own board is in the walls trying to undermine my leadership...
Do the voices you hear sound like your own voice or like they are coming from other people?

Oh, no, no, definitely not my own voice. Like I was just saying a moment ago—and this is what makes the whole situation so incredibly disruptive to my workflow—it is distinctly the voices of other people. Specifically, the board members and my senior staff. 

I can hear Arthur, for instance—he's the chairman of the board, he has this very distinct, gravelly baritone voice—and I hear him plain as day coming right through the screen of my powered-down phone. And then Sarah, my VP of Operations, I hear her higher-pitched voice chiming in right behind him, agreeing that I'm ruining the company and destroying everything we've built. So it's absolutely not my own thoughts or my own voice echoing or anything like that. It is them. 

I know their voices intimately. I've sat in hundreds of hours of meetings with these people, negotiating contracts, planning our entire fiscal year, so when I hear them dissecting my strategic decisions through the drywall of the executive conference room, I know exactly who is speaking. That's exactly why I end up answering them out loud! I'll literally be sitting at my desk and say, 'Arthur, you personally signed off on this expansion in Q2,' because it sounds exactly like he's standing two feet away from me, breathing down my neck. It's only after I've started defending myself that I realize... well, like I said before, that no one else in the office heard it and the room is actually empty. But it is unequivocally their voices, clear as a bell, not mine.
Do you hear these voices only when you're in the conference room or near your office, or can you hear them at other times and places as well?

Well, that’s... that's the thing that's really starting to become a problem, honestly. At first, it was just the office. Just the executive floor. I'd be at my desk, looking over the quarterly reports, and I'd hear Arthur or Sarah through the drywall of the conference room, or coming out of my phone when it was completely powered down and black on my desk. Just going on and on about how I'm ruining the company, destroying everything we've built. And like I said, it was so clear I'd literally speak out loud to answer them before I realized no one else heard it. 

But lately... lately it's not just the office. I'll be in my car, driving home, right? The radio is completely off because I need silence to decompress after a twelve-hour day, and suddenly, coming right through the air conditioning vents, I hear them. Arthur's gravelly voice, clear as day, criticizing my handling of the recent merger. Or I'll be at home, in my own kitchen, making a cup of coffee at six in the morning, and I'll hear Sarah's voice coming from the microwave, telling me my financial strategy is a disaster. 

It’s completely inescapable. I mean, how am I supposed to maintain my focus, how am I supposed to run a Fortune 500 company, when my board members are somehow broadcasting their criticisms into my car and my kitchen appliances? It's just... it's everywhere now. The walls at work, the phone when it's off, the vents, the appliances... I just can't get away from them saying I'm ruining the company. And I still—I still catch myself answering back, even when I'm standing alone in my kitchen in my bathrobe. I'll be explaining my fiscal logic to the microwave before I realize, again, that no one else is there. It's just... it's highly disruptive to my entire life at this point, not just my workflow.
Do the voices you hear tell you to do specific things or are they just criticizing your decisions?

Well, no, they don't exactly give me orders, if that's what you mean. They aren't telling me to, I don't know, sign a specific contract or fire someone. It's really just this relentless, constant barrage of criticism. Like I was saying, it's the board members and my staff—Arthur, Sarah, the others—and they just keep talking about me. Always about me, and always about how I'm ruining the company. 

I mean, I'll be trying to draft a memo, and I hear them coming right through the conference room walls, or like I mentioned, from my phone when it's completely powered down and sitting face down on my desk. They just go on and on, dissecting every choice I've made. "She's destroying everything we've built," or "Her Q3 projections are a complete fantasy," things like that. It's a running commentary on my supposed failures as a chief executive. 

And they never tell me *what* to do instead, which is incredibly frustrating from a management perspective. If you're going to criticize my financial strategy, at least offer an alternative, right? But no, it's just this endless chorus of them saying I'm ruining the company. And the clarity of it—I really can't emphasize enough how clear it sounds. It's not whispering. It's so distinct that, as I told you, I will literally stop what I'm doing and answer them out loud. I'll start defending my decisions, arguing with Arthur about the profit margins, and I get so caught up in the debate before it finally hits me that... that no one else in the room heard it, and they aren't actually there. But they don't give me commands, no. Just... just the constant, inescapable criticism.
How are these voices and your responses to them affecting your relationships with your board members and staff in real life?

Well, it's... it's completely eroding everything, to be completely honest with you. I mean, you can probably imagine the tension, right? If I'm sitting in a real, actual, scheduled board meeting with Arthur and Sarah, and I'm sitting at the head of the table glaring at them because I think they just spent the last three hours trashing my Q3 projections through the air conditioning vents... it makes things incredibly strained. I'm defensive before the meeting even begins. 

But the real issue, the thing that is just devastating to admit, is that because of all this constant noise and disruption, I am just no longer reliably able to run the division. I mean, I used to pride myself on my decisiveness. I built this division, I know every moving part, every supply chain metric, every fiscal loophole. But now? I sit down to look at the quarterly financials, or I try to review a basic merger contract, and I just can't keep up with basic executive decisions anymore. It takes me days to approve a simple vendor agreement because I'm constantly having to stop what I'm doing, put my pen down, and defend my logic out loud to an empty room. 

And they know it. The staff, I mean. They see me slipping, they hear me talking back to my powered-down phone, or they see me staring blankly at a spreadsheet for hours. So they've started... well, my senior staff have quietly taken over work I used to handle myself. Sarah, especially. I'll go to pull a report to analyze the margins, and I'll find out she already finalized it and sent it directly to Arthur. They don't say anything to my face, they don't confront me, they just... route the emails around me now. They're managing the company around me. It's incredibly humiliating to see my own senior staff just bypassing the chief executive because I can't function properly. 

And the worst part is that it doesn't even stop when I leave the building, so my entire life is taking a hit. When I get home, I am so completely drained from fighting these phantom criticisms all day that I have nothing left. My husband has had to step in and manage practically all of the household responsibilities. I used to be so organized, you know, I ran our home with the same efficiency as my office. But now... I'll go to the kitchen to start making dinner, I'll hear Sarah criticizing my leadership from the microwave, and I just walk away. I leave things completely unfinished. Or, more often than not lately, I just do not start them at all. My husband is doing the cooking, paying the bills, managing the house, because I'm too busy arguing with people who aren't even in the room to remember to turn on the stove. It's just... everything is slipping through my fingers, everywhere.
Do you ever feel like you're outside of your body, watching yourself react to these voices?

No, I... I can't say I've ever felt anything like that. I mean, I know what you're describing, like that floating feeling people talk about where they're watching themselves from the ceiling or something, but no. It's actually the exact opposite for me. I am painfully, acutely aware of being right there in my own skin when it happens. 

When I hear Arthur's voice coming through the air conditioning vents, I don't detach at all. I feel my heart rate spike, my palms get clammy, I feel this intense tension in my jaw from clenching my teeth. I am so firmly planted in my own body, sitting right there in my ergonomic chair at my desk, feeling every single ounce of the stress and the indignation. I honestly wish I *could* just float away and watch it from the outside, because maybe then it wouldn't be so completely exhausting. But no, I am very much present. I feel the weight of the pen in my hand right before I throw it down on the desk to argue back. I feel the cold tile under my feet in the kitchen when I'm standing there in my bathrobe, yelling at the microwave about supply chain logistics. 

It's all happening directly to me, right in the moment. There's no separation, no distance at all. It's just this heavy, crushing reality of being me, right there, having to defend my entire career and my intelligence to empty space. And it takes such a physical toll, you know? The adrenaline, the constant state of fight-or-flight... my shoulders are practically glued to my ears by the end of the day from the sheer physical tension of it all. So, no, I'm completely trapped inside myself while this is happening. I'm not outside of my body at all, I'm just... I'm stuck right in the middle of it.
Have you ever experienced anything like this before, where you heard voices or had similar thoughts?

No, never. Never in my entire life, which is why this is all so completely baffling to me. I mean, before this... this current situation, I have always been the most grounded, rational person you could ever meet. You don't get to be a chief executive by having an overactive imagination, right? You deal in facts, in data, in hard numbers. So for my entire life, my mind has been my sharpest tool, completely clear, completely under my control. 

But this? The voices coming from the walls, or from my phone when it's powered down... that has only been happening for about the past three months. I remember exactly when it started, actually, because it was right around the end of the second quarter. We were doing the mid-year financial reviews, and I was sitting in my office late one Tuesday evening. I had the quarterly reports spread out all over my desk—the big mahogany one my husband bought me when I got the promotion—and that was the very first time I heard Arthur's voice coming from the receiver of my dead cell phone. I had forgotten my charger at home, the screen was completely black, and suddenly there he was, criticizing my handling of a logistics contract. 

Since that night, it's just been a steady escalation. First it was just the phone, and then a few weeks later it started coming through the walls, the air conditioning vents in the conference room, and then the microwave at home like I mentioned earlier. It's been about three months of this absolute relentless nightmare. I keep trying to trace it back, you know? I sit there and try to analyze it like a business problem, trying to figure out if there was some warning sign four months ago or five months ago, maybe a particularly stressful week or a bad quarter that I somehow missed. But there wasn't. It just started out of nowhere three months ago, and it hasn't stopped for a single day since. So, no, absolutely nothing like this before. Just these last three months.
Have you ever had any other episodes in your life where you experienced similar breaks from reality?

No. No, absolutely not. Like I... like I was just trying to explain a minute ago, this is completely unprecedented for me. I have never, not once in my forty-three years, experienced anything that you could even remotely call a break from reality. 

I mean, my entire life, my entire career, has been built on being the person in the room who is the most anchored to reality. When I left college early to start working, I had to be twice as sharp, twice as focused as everyone else with a fancy degree just to get a foot in the door. I didn't have the luxury of losing touch with what was real. I built my way up to chief executive by looking at the hard facts, the market trends, the profit margins—things you can touch, things you can prove on a piece of paper. 

So, no, there were no other episodes. Not in my twenties, not in my thirties. I've never had a breakdown, I've never heard things, I've never even taken a mental health day because I felt overwhelmed. My mind has always been a steel trap. I remember every vendor contract, every senior staff member's performance review from the last decade. I am the one who fixes things when other people panic. So to have you ask if I've had other breaks from reality... I mean, I understand why you have to ask, it's your job and I know what this looks like, but it almost feels absurd to even consider it. 

Until three months ago, I was the most fiercely rational person I knew. My husband used to joke that I was practically a machine when it came to logic and keeping our lives on track. So this... this whole nightmare with the voices and the constant sabotage... this is the very first time my brain has ever betrayed me like this. There is absolutely nothing in my past, no history, no warning signs, nothing that could have predicted this happening to me. It's just these last three months, and that's it.
Was there a particularly stressful or traumatic event in the months leading up to when you first started hearing the voices?

Stressful? I mean... yes and no. It wasn't just a single isolated event, you know, not like a car crash or a sudden death in the family or something you could just circle in red on a calendar and say, 'There, that's the trauma.' It was more like... a pressure cooker. If I really sit back and analyze the trajectory of it all, the absolute crushing weight of the pressure... this has actually been building for about two years and four months. 

That was when the board approved the major company expansion. And, of course, because of my track record, because I always, always deliver on my metrics, they put me in charge of the new arts-and-commerce division. 

You have absolutely no idea the logistical nightmare that was. Trying to bridge the gap between creative directors who don't understand basic profit margins and corporate stakeholders who only care about the bottom line... it was like trying to speak two completely different languages at the same time. I was working eighty, sometimes ninety-hour weeks. I had to oversee the entire integration, the hiring, the restructuring of the supply chains. I mean, I was flying to different regional offices almost every other day. I practically lived in airport lounges and sterile hotel rooms, eating terrible lukewarm room service while reviewing merger documents at two in the morning. 

Everyone kept saying, 'Oh, you're doing such a brilliant job, you're the only one who can handle this transition,' but the sheer volume of the responsibility was just astronomical. I was the linchpin holding a multi-million dollar expansion together. I remember the exact month it all started, actually, because it was right after my forty-first birthday, and my husband had planned this beautiful, quiet weekend getaway to the coast that I had to cancel at the absolute last minute because the new regional managers couldn't figure out the integrated payroll system. I just couldn't step away. I had to be the one to fix it. I always have to fix it. 

So, yes, the voices—the stuff with Arthur and the air conditioning vents—like I said, that specific nightmare started three months ago at the end of Q2. But the foundation for all of this? The absolute exhaustion and the feeling that I was constantly under a microscope, constantly having to defend my decisions? That has been brewing for exactly two years and four months, ever since that expansion launched and I took over arts-and-commerce. It's just been this relentless, compounding stress, day after day, building and building and building until... well, until three months ago.
Do you find it difficult to organize your thoughts or express them in a coherent manner when responding to the voices?

Difficult to organize my thoughts? No. No, not at all. If anything, I am hyper-organized when I respond to them. When Arthur, or whoever else decides to chime in from the vents, starts critiquing my decisions, I don't just sit there and fall apart. I am a chief executive. I respond the exact same way I would in a boardroom full of hostile shareholders. 

I mean, my thoughts are perfectly clear. I lay out the facts. Just the other day, when he was going on and on about the Q3 projections while I was trying to make my morning coffee, I actually stopped, put down my mug, and verbally dismantled his entire argument point by point. I told him that the profit margins on the arts-and-commerce division are solid, the overhead is accounted for, and I cited the exact spreadsheet cells right back at the microwave. 

So, no, I don't lose my train of thought or get confused. My mind is just as sharp as it always is. It's actually incredibly frustrating because I am making completely coherent, logically sound arguments, and it's like talking to a brick wall. Or, well, literally talking to a wall, I suppose. But my point is, I know exactly what I want to say. I have the data, I have the rationale, and I articulate it perfectly. I don't stumble over my words. I don't get flustered. I just... I just have to constantly defend myself against these completely baseless accusations, and I do it with the exact same clarity and precision that got me my job in the first place. So if you're asking if my brain is turning to mush or if I can't string a sentence together when they speak to me, the answer is absolutely not. I am completely, one hundred percent lucid when I tell them exactly why they are wrong.
Have you ever had any other experiences where you heard voices or saw things that weren't there before these past three months?

No. No, absolutely not. I know I was just talking about the timeline a few minutes ago, but I really need to emphasize this because I feel like you're searching for some kind of lifelong pattern that simply does not exist. I have never, ever experienced anything like this before. No voices, no seeing things, no... whatever else you might be looking for in my past. I am a very grounded, practical person. If I had been hearing things five years ago, or ten years ago, I wouldn't have been able to negotiate half the corporate mergers I did. I wouldn't have been able to function at the executive level. 

So, no. It is strictly, exclusively tied to this recent window. It has only been for about the past three months. That is the exact, verifiable timeline. Before that, my office was just an office. My smartphone was just a tool I used to communicate with my regional directors and my board. But for the past three months, that's when it all started—the voices coming directly out of the walls, or coming through the earpiece on my phone when there isn't even an active call on the line. 

I'll just be sitting there at my desk, completely alone, reviewing a quarterly report, and suddenly the drywall is criticizing my resource allocation. Or I'll pick up my cell to check an email and I can hear them whispering through the speaker, second-guessing my authority. It's incredibly distracting, especially when you're trying to manage a multi-million dollar division. But before three months ago? Nothing. Complete silence. Just the normal sounds of a functioning business and a normal life. I pride myself on my memory, doctor, I track data and spot anomalies for a living, so you can trust me when I tell you that this specific issue, these voices from the walls and my phone, have been happening for about three months and not a single day longer.
Have you ever used any recreational drugs or had problems with alcohol?

Recreational drugs? Alcohol problems? I mean... frankly, I find the suggestion almost comical. I know you have a checklist and you probably have to ask everyone who walks through your door, but... no. Absolutely not. Do you have any idea what my daily schedule looks like? I am managing a multi-million dollar division. You cannot do what I do—you cannot survive in the C-suite—if you are clouding your judgment with substances. 

Take alcohol, for instance. Do I attend corporate dinners? Yes. Do I host galas and networking events for the arts-and-commerce sector? Of course I do. And in those environments, there is always a sommelier, there is always some two-hundred-dollar bottle of Cabernet being poured, or an open bar with top-shelf liquor. But I will have exactly one glass. Or, really, half a glass. I hold it by the stem, I take a polite sip during the quarterly toast, and then I set it down and I leave it there for the rest of the night. You just cannot afford to lose your edge. If you have one too many martinis at a vendor dinner, you might slip up. You might verbally agree to a contract term that hasn't been vetted by legal, or you might show weakness in front of a rival regional manager. I've actually seen it happen. I watched a VP of marketing completely derail his entire career trajectory at a holiday party a few years ago because he couldn't handle his scotch. I told myself right then and there, I will never, ever let myself be that vulnerable. 

And as for recreational drugs? Please. I don't even have time to get a full six hours of sleep most nights, let alone sit around doing... whatever it is people do when they're high. I need my mind to be a steel trap. I have to process hundreds of data points, logistical frameworks, supply chain metrics, all simultaneously. My brain is my greatest asset. I don't even like taking over-the-counter cold medicine if I have the sniffles because I absolutely despise that fuzzy, lethargic feeling it gives you. I need absolute, uncompromised clarity at all times. I have to be sharper than everyone else in the room just to maintain my position. So, no. No drugs, no drinking problems. The only thing I consume in excess is quarterly reports.
Have you experienced any other unusual sensations or perceptions, such as seeing things that aren't there, besides hearing the voices?

Seeing things? No. No, I don't see things. My vision is perfectly fine, 20/20. I’m not seeing shadows or people who aren't there or whatever else you might be fishing for. It is strictly what I’ve been telling you about. In fact, that’s the entire reason I even agreed to come in here and speak with you, because of what I keep hearing. 

And I really need you to understand the mechanics of this, because it’s not just some vague, random noise in the distance. It is highly specific and incredibly disruptive. I’ll be sitting in the main conference room, perhaps reviewing a pitch deck or going over the quarterly budget, and I will hear them talking about me right through the conference room walls. And it’s not just anyone—it’s usually the board members, or sometimes my own upper-level staff, people whose salaries I personally approve. They just relentlessly go on and on about how I’m ruining the company. They critique my strategies, they say I'm driving our market share into the ground, which is statistically absurd if you actually look at our year-over-year growth. 

Or it happens with my phone. I’ll have my phone sitting right there on my desk, completely off—I mean powered down, screen black, not even in standby mode—and I can hear them coming right through the speaker. And doctor, it sounds so incredibly clear. The acoustics, the inflection, the sheer disrespect in their delivery... it is so real that I actually answer them. I will literally sit there and argue back. I'll start defending my fiscal policies out loud to the room, pointing out the flaws in their logic, and I’ll be two or three minutes into a very articulate, forceful defense before I suddenly stop and realize... no one else heard it. My executive assistant will just be sitting right outside my glass door, typing away, completely oblivious. But the voices are so vivid, so physically present in the room with me, that my immediate reflex is to manage them just like I would any insubordinate employee. 

So, no, I don't see things. But what I am hearing is so precise and so loud that I am actively having full conversations with them before it even dawns on me that the room is technically empty.
Do you think the voices you hear are real or are they just a product of your own mind?

Real or my mind? I mean... look, that is exactly the paradox I am dealing with here, and it's incredibly frustrating. Like I was just trying to explain to you a second ago, the entire reason I came in here to see you is because I keep hearing these people talking about me through the conference room walls, or coming out of my phone even when it is completely powered off. And it's not just random noise, it’s my board members or my upper-level staff specifically saying that I am ruining the company. 

So, my logical, executive brain knows that a powered-down piece of electronics cannot transmit an audio signal. I know that. I went to college, I understand basic physics and telecommunications. But when you ask if it's real? Doctor, in the moment it is happening, it is absolute reality. It sounds so perfectly, acoustically clear that I answer them. I literally argue back. I will stand there and defend my fiscal decisions out loud, and it's only after I've been talking for a few minutes that I stop and realize... no one else heard it. My assistant sitting right outside didn't hear a single thing. 

So, to answer your question... after the fact, when I'm sitting here in this chair analyzing the data, I have to deduce that it must be some sort of... misfiring or product of my own mind, because the room is technically empty. I know the laws of reality. But when I am in that conference room? When I hear the CFO's exact voice dripping with condescension coming right through the plaster? It is entirely real to me. I wouldn't be having full-blown, aggressive arguments with a wall if it didn't sound completely, undeniably authentic. I just wouldn't. I'm too smart for that. And that is exactly why this is so disruptive to my schedule.
Have you ever had any other episodes in your life where you heard voices or experienced similar hallucinations before these past three months?

Before these past three months? No. No, absolutely not. I mean, if I had been dealing with this kind of... disruption earlier in my career, there is simply no way I would have climbed the corporate ladder the way I did. You have to understand, my entire professional life has been built on precision. On clarity. I've always been the person in the room who can hear a pin drop, who can read the subtext of a negotiation, who knows exactly what is being said and what isn't. So to have this happen... it's completely unprecedented for me. 

It really just started about three months ago. That's when I first noticed it. I remember the exact week, actually, because we were in the middle of closing Q3, and I was going over the preliminary EBITDA margins, and suddenly... there it was. The voices from the walls. And then, a few days later, it was coming from my phone. At first, I thought it was some sort of bizarre acoustic anomaly in the building, or maybe a crossed wire in the telecom system. I even had IT come up and run a diagnostic on the entire executive suite because I was so convinced someone had tapped the lines or installed some sort of rogue speaker system. But, of course, they found nothing. 

And for the past three months, it has just been this relentless... barrage. Day in and day out. But before that? Never. Not once. My mind has always been my greatest asset, completely untouchable. That's why this last quarter has been so incredibly frustrating, because I am not used to second-guessing my own sensory input. Three months of this is already three months too long, frankly.
Have you noticed any changes in your sleep patterns over the past few months?

Sleep? No... no, I wouldn't say my sleep has changed. I mean, you have to understand, I've never been someone who needs a solid eight hours of rest. You simply don't get to the C-suite by sleeping half the day away. I have always operated on a very strict, highly regimented schedule. I usually leave the office around 7 PM, have a working dinner, review the Asian market opens, and I am in bed by midnight. And then I am up at 4:30 AM sharp. Every single day. I don't even use an alarm clock anymore, my circadian rhythm is just completely dialed in to my professional obligations. 

So, even with all this... absolute chaos happening at the office during the day, once I actually get home to my penthouse and get into my own bed, I sleep exactly the same as I always have. I mean, I might be a bit more mentally exhausted by the end of the day right now, because, frankly, having to verbally defend my fiscal strategies to an empty room is incredibly draining. It takes a massive amount of energy to manage that level of perceived insubordination, even if it is just... whatever we're calling it, a misfiring of my brain. You get home and you're just depleted. 

But the actual mechanics of my sleep? The duration, the quality? No, that hasn't changed at all. I still close my eyes, I get my four and a half hours of deep sleep, and I wake up ready to tackle the quarterly projections just like I did five years ago. I'm very disciplined about my downtime. So, no, to answer your question, there hasn't been any shift in my sleep patterns.
Do you find it hard to keep your thoughts straight or express them in a way that makes sense when you're not hearing the voices?

Keep my thoughts straight? No. No, absolutely not. I mean... if anything, my thoughts are almost too organized, if that makes sense. When I’m not dealing with the... the auditory interruptions, my mind is completely sharp. It’s a steel trap. You have to understand, my entire role as a chief executive requires me to take massive amounts of complex data—you know, market analytics, internal restructuring proposals, risk assessments—and synthesize all of that into very clear, very actionable directives for my team. 

I am constantly communicating. Constantly. I lead board meetings where I have to speak for forty-five minutes straight, entirely without notes, just laying out the strategic vision for the next fiscal year. And I do it flawlessly. People actually compliment me on how articulate I am, how I can take a completely chaotic situation and explain it in a way that makes absolute sense to everyone in the room. So, no, my thoughts aren't jumbled. I don't lose my train of thought, I don't... I don't struggle to find the right words. 

It's only when I'm sitting there trying to review a vendor contract and suddenly I hear the VP of Marketing whispering through the air vent that I'm driving the stock price down... that is when I get derailed. Because obviously, I have to stop what I'm doing and address that insubordination immediately. But the underlying machinery of my mind? The way I process and express information when the room is actually quiet? It is completely intact. If I couldn't communicate clearly, the board would have replaced me months ago, frankly. So, no, I don't have any issue keeping my thoughts straight whatsoever.
Was there a specific event or situation in the months or years leading up to when you first heard the voices that you found particularly stressful or traumatic?

Stressful? Traumatic? No... no, I wouldn't use those words. I mean, look, my entire career is built on stress, if you want to call it that. When you're managing a global portfolio, overseeing hundreds of employees, and answering directly to a board of directors who only care about quarterly growth, stress is just... it's just the baseline operating temperature. It's the air I breathe. I don't even register it as stress anymore, it's just Tuesday, you know? 

So, in the months leading up to Q3, when this all started... no, there wasn't any singular, catastrophic event. There was no trauma. I didn't lose a loved one, I wasn't in a car accident, the company wasn't facing a hostile takeover. It was just business as usual. We were gearing up for the end of the fiscal year, which is always a high-stakes environment, but it's an environment I thrive in. I've been doing this for over a decade.
